title: Tenant Egress Bandwidth Burst-Shaper & Fairness Implementation
author: Maya Thompson
body:
Summary

This document describes a pragmatic implementation for per-tenant egress bandwidth shaping with burst allowances and fairness guarantees. The solution is intended for Redwood's multi-tenant GPU service endpoints and control-plane egress paths. It balances predictable billing/SLAs, short-term burstiness for customer UX, and efficient utilization of constrained egress capacity to reduce cross-tenant interference.

Goals

- Limit per-tenant sustained egress (Mbps) while permitting short bursts for onboarding/interactive workloads.
- Ensure fairness during contention windows (no single tenant can starve others).
- Provide Terraform modules and deployment recipes that work on AWS and GCP-hosted VPC egress gateways.
- Integrate with existing observability (Prometheus metrics + Grafana dashboards) and alerting.

Non-goals

- This doc does not attempt to replace cloud-provider traffic shaping primitives for tenant isolation at the VM hypervisor-level.
- Not a network-level DDoS defense plan; combine with DDoS protections and WAFs.

Terminology

- Tenant: Billing/identity boundary (customer account).
- Egress gateway: A NAT/egress-host responsible for routing tenant outbound flows to the internet or partner clouds.
- Shaper: Policing/queuing construct used to enforce bandwidth limits (e.g., Linux tc, cloud traffic shaping, or managed NAT gateway QoS).

Architecture overview

We operate a pool of egress gateways per-region. Each gateway services multiple tenant subnets via SNAT prefixes. The shaper is applied at the gateway host interface to enforce per-tenant limits. Key components:

- Tenant tagging: We rely on SNAT IP allocation per-tenant (or per-tenant ENI) to map flows back to tenant identity.
- Shaping plane: Linux tc qdiscs per-tenant veth/iptables mark pipeline (or cloud BPF-based filter where available).
- Controller: A Terraform-managed controller that pushes tenant quotas and burst profiles to gateways via a small control agent (grpc/HTTP).
- Telemetry: Per-tenant egress metrics exported to Prometheus (bytes/sec, drops, queue depth, burst tokens).

Design choices and rationale

- SNAT-by-tenant mapping is simpler than deep packet inspection and scales with cloud NAT design. It also aligns with billing and IPAM.
- Use Hierarchical Token Bucket (HTB) for guaranteed rates and CBQ/ fq_codel for fairness in bursts. HTB lets us set a rate and ceiling (burst).
- Keep shaper config small (<= 12 classes/gateway) to avoid control plane churn. For very high tenant counts, use per-tenant load-balancing across gateways and aggregate shaping per-tenant group.

Configuration matrix (recommended defaults)

| Parameter | Low-tier | Mid-tier | High-tier | Notes |
|-----------|---------:|---------:|---------:|-------|
| sustained_rate | 50 Mbps | 200 Mbps | 1 Gbps | Default sustained throughput per tenant class |
| burst_window | 10s | 20s | 60s | How long tenant can exceed sustained_rate up to ceiling |
| burst_ceiling | 200 Mbps | 800 Mbps | 2 Gbps | Peak allowed during burst window |
| monitoring_interval | 30s | 30s | 15s | Prometheus scrape target for egress metrics |
| enforcement_mode | shaping | shaping | shaping+policing | policing drops if exceeded beyond burst_window |

Terraform module: recommended pattern

Use a small module (egress-shaper) that manages: allocation of SNAT pools, IAM roles for gateways to fetch configs, and a configmap for the controller. Example usage (HCL-like illustration):

```
module "egress_shaper" {
  source = "git::ssh://git@github.com/redwood/infra-modules.git//egress-shaper"
  region = "us-west-2"
  gateway_count = 3
  tenant_classes = {
    "free"  = { sustained_rate = "50mbit"  , burst_ceiling = "200mbit", burst_window="10s" }
    "pro"   = { sustained_rate = "200mbit" , burst_ceiling = "800mbit", burst_window="20s" }
    "ent"   = { sustained_rate = "1gbit"   , burst_ceiling = "2gbit"  , burst_window="60s" }
  }
}
```

Notes: module produces: k/v store entries, gateway bootstrap userdata that includes the controller agent endpoint and a TLS client cert secret. The module does NOT deploy the controller; that is a separate service (see infra-services repo).

Linux tc example (gateway host)

Below is a tested pattern for a gateway that maps SNAT IPs to tc class IDs via iptables MARKs. The example is illustrative — production deployment should use the controller to push rules.

1) Create root HTB qdisc on eth0: 

sudo tc qdisc add dev eth0 root handle 1: htb default 999
sudo tc class add dev eth0 parent 1: classid 1:1 htb rate 10gbit

2) Per-tenant class and filter (tenant SNAT IP = 198.51.100.42):

sudo tc class add dev eth0 parent 1:1 classid 1:100 htb rate 200mbit ceil 2gbit burst 1600k
sudo tc qdisc add dev eth0 parent 1:100 handle 1000: fq_codel
sudo iptables -t mangle -A POSTROUTING -s 10.0.42.0/24 -j MARK --set-mark 100
sudo tc filter add dev eth0 protocol ip parent 1:0 prio 1 handle 100 fw flowid 1:100

3) Token-bucket like behavior: CBQ token bucket is emulated with HTB + ceil; adjust burst and quantum for latency-sensitive workloads.

Cloud-specific notes

- AWS: Use per-tenant ENIs or Elastic IP pools for SNAT where possible. AWS-managed NAT gateways do not expose qdisc controls; forwarding through our own gateway (EC2 or ENI-based appliances) gives full control. Consider using host-based ENIs and SSM for agent orchestration.
- GCP: Use Cloud NAT or self-managed NAT instances. For very high throughput, deploy BPF-based eBPF shapers (Cilium) at the node-level.

Monitoring and observability

Export the following per-tenant metrics to Prometheus (gateway exporter):
- redwood_egress_tx_bytes_total{tenant_id, gateway}
- redwood_egress_tx_rate_mbps{tenant_id, gateway}
- redwood_egress_queue_depth_bytes{tenant_id, gateway}
- redwood_egress_drops_total{tenant_id, gateway, reason}
- redwood_egress_burst_tokens{tenant_id, gateway}
Example Grafana panels to create:
- Top 10 tenants by sustained 5m tx rate (rate(redwood_egress_tx_bytes_total[5m]))
- Tenant fairness heatmap (per-tenant deviation vs class mean)
- Gateway resource pressure (CPU, netdev qlen, socket usage)

Alerts (recommended)

- P1: Gateway queue depth > 75% for > 5m (critical) — action: scale gateways, engage networking oncall.
- P2: Tenant sustained_rate > 3x configured sustained for > 10m (billing + abuse) — action: contact CS + rate-limited throttling.
- P3: Drops rate > 5% of bytes for > 2m — action: investigate shaping misconfiguration.

Operational runbook (incident flow)

1) Detection: Alert fires for queue_depth > 75% on gateway G.
2) Triage: 
   a) Identify top 5 offending tenants: query Prometheus for top tenants by rate on G for last 10m.
   b) If a single tenant is responsible and exceeds denom thresholds, temporarily cap burst_ceiling via controller to sustained_rate for that tenant class.
   c) If multiple tenants are crowding, scale up gateway pool (see scaling section) or move noisy tenants to alternate gateways.
3) Remediation: 
   - To reduce immediate pressure: increase root HTB parent rate (if headroom on host NIC), or move tenants by updating SNAT pool allocation (Terraform plan -> apply).
   - To enforce strict limits: flip enforcement_mode to policing (drops) for offending tenant class. Coordinate with CS to notify customers.
4) Post-incident: 
   - Run a fairness report (script in infra-tools) for affected time window and attach to incident timeline.
   - Adjust default sustained_rate or burst parameters if pattern recurs.

Scaling and placement guidance

- Gateway sizing: provision NICs and instance types to support aggregated peak CEIL across tenants with 20% headroom. For example, a c6i.4xlarge with enhanced networking supports ~10 Gbps sustained; use multiple NICs for >10 Gbps.
- Tenant placement: use tenant locality to minimize cross-region egress; prefer assigning tenant's SNAT pool to gateways in the tenant's most-used region.
- Autoscaling: When CPU or netdev qlen > 70% for 2 consecutive 60s cycles, scale +1 gateway in the group (bounded by gateway_count max). Automate with controller and Terraform or cloud autoscaling groups.

Testing checklist (pre-deploy)

1) Unit tests for controller: config push, rollback, and idempotency.
2) Integration test: simulate 50 tenants with 10% noisy tenants; verify compliance with sustained and burst limits.
3) Chaos test: kill one gateway to ensure traffic reassigns and that fairness holds across remaining gateways.
4) Cost test: measure egress billing delta before/after shaping for a 72h window.

Appendix: useful commands and scripts

- psuedo-query: Top tenants by 5m rate
  curl -s "http://prometheus/api/v1/query?query=topk(10,rate(redwood_egress_tx_bytes_total[5m]))" | jq .

- Quick toggle to policing for class 1: (via controller API):
  curl -X POST https://controller.us-west-2.redwood.internal/v1/shaper/tenant/100/mode -d '{"mode":"policing"}' -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN"

- Terraform apply sequence:
  1) terraform plan -var-file=prod.tfvars
  2) terraform apply -auto-approve -var-file=prod.tfvars
